Add one analysis for each scenario and simulation to a plan

Source: R/plan.R
add_analyses.Rd

add_analyses() adds the analysis kind name to the plnr plan p: one analysis for each scenario and simulation of scenarios, and for each combination of the extra dimensions in ....

Usage

add_analyses(p, scenarios, name, fn, ..., control = FALSE)

Arguments

p

A plan from plnr::Plan$new().

scenarios

The scenarios of the run, from scenarios().

name

The name of the analysis kind, for example "models". It is the name of the element of the results object. It MUST be a syntactic name that starts with a letter. It MUST NOT be "manifest" or "exclusions", and it MUST NOT start with "pbn_". Each kind of one plan MUST have its own name. save_results() names the exclusion table of a cohort exclusions.

fn

The action function, function(data, argset).

...

The extra dimensions, each named, for example outcome = CFG$outcomes. Each MUST be an atomic vector with at least one value, with no NA and no value twice. A vector of length 1 is a constant of the kind.

control

TRUE adds the kind to every fake scenario of scenarios, and never to "real". Use it for a check that is not a result, for example a model without adjustment that a fake scenario tests.

Value

Invisibly, the names of the analyses of the kind, in the order of the plan.

Details

Each analysis gets the name <scenario>__sim_<kkkk>__<name>__<i>, for example null__sim_0003__models__2. <kkkk> is the simulation with four digits, also for a scenario with 1 simulation. <i> counts the combinations of the extra dimensions from 1, with the last dimension of ... changing fastest. A kind without extra dimensions has <i> 1. To step through one analysis by hand, use get_argset() and get_data(). They take the scenario, the simulation, the kind and <i>, so you do not type the name.

The argset of each analysis holds these fields:

  • scenario, sim, and analysis, the kind name.

  • seed, the seed of the analysis.

  • the value of each extra dimension.

  • the value of each setting column of its scenario.

The name of an extra dimension MUST follow these rules:

  • It MUST be syntactic.

  • It MUST NOT be the name of a setting column.

  • It MUST NOT be one of scenario, sim, analysis, seed, index_analysis, name, fn, fn_name, data and argset.

pbn adds fn in a wrapper. The wrapper calls set.seed(argset$seed) and then fn(data, argset). fn runs inside the wrapper, so plnr::is_run_directly() is FALSE in it when the plan runs.

The seed depends on the kind name, the counter <i> and sim only:

  • It does not depend on the order of the analyses, the worker count or the R session.

  • Two kinds of one simulation get different seeds, so they draw different numbers.

  • One kind gets the same seed in each scenario, so its draws in null and in real of one simulation are the same.

  • It is 10000 or more, so it differs from the seed sim of the data of simulations 1 to 9999.

The seed is 10000 + h %% 2147473629. h is a polynomial hash with base 257, modulo the prime 2147483629, of the code points of "<name>__<i>__<sim>". Two analyses of one simulation with the same seed stop add_analyses() with an error that names both kinds.

While run_plan() runs, an analysis fails when it changes the shared data in place. plnr gives every analysis of one scenario and simulation the same object, so a later analysis in the same R session would get the changed data. pbn compares two things before and after each analysis:

  • the names, the number of rows, the data.table key and the address of each column of each data.frame. This finds an added, removed, renamed or replaced column, for example data$d[, x := 1], and a new key from data.table::setkey().

  • a hash of the values and the attributes of each column of each data.frame, and of each data.frame in a list of data.frames. The attributes of such a list, such as its names, have a hash too. This finds a change of values in place. Examples are data$d[1, x := 0], data$d[g == "a", y := NA] and data.table::set() on some rows. It also finds data.table::setorder(), and data.table::setattr() on a column or on the table. The error names the data and each changed column.

The hash leaves out the index that a data.table subset such as data$d[g == "a"] adds to the table, because the index changes no value.

Each other data element, for example a vector or a model, gets one hash of its whole value. The error then names the data and says "in its value". That hash leaves out each function in the value and the contents of each environment in it, such as that of a formula. R changes a function when it compiles it, so a read could look like a change. pbn does not check a data element that is a function or an environment, also an R6 object. Copy the data first with data.table::copy() when the analysis changes it, or make the change in a data step.

pbn hashes each data object before its first analysis in an R session, and after each analysis. An analysis that changes the data fails and stops the run, so the first hash holds for each later analysis. The time grows with the size of the data. On one computer, the hash after an analysis took 0.07 s for a data.table with one million rows and 20 columns of mixed types. It took 0.03 s for ten million rows and 5 numeric columns. The same data as a plain data.frame took 0.10 s and 0.23 s. The first analysis of each data object costs a second hash.

While run_plan() runs, an analysis also fails when it changes an object of the functions folder, for example CFG. plnr runs many analyses in one R session, so the change would reach each later analysis of that session. A result would then depend on the analyses that ran before it there. pbn checks each object that the functions folder made or changed when initialize_project() sourced it, other than a function, a plnr plan and .Random.seed. It compares the bytes of serialize() of each object before and after the analysis. That finds a new value, a new element and a new attribute. It compares them before and after each data function or data step too. A data function that changes such an object fails each analysis that gets its data. The error names the first top-level element that changed, for example CFG$table. It also says how: a new attribute such as the index of a data.table, a new or a gone element, or another value. The output function of make_outputs() and each expect_ function of save_results() get the same check in this R session.

While run_plan() runs, two more parts of the state of an R session cannot pass from one analysis to the next:

  • An analysis fails when it leaves a new object in the global environment, for example with <<- or assign(). .Random.seed does not count.

  • pbn takes the kind of random number generator of the run from RNGkind() at the start of run_plan(). It sets that kind again before each seed of a data function and of an analysis. An analysis that calls RNGkind() then changes no draw of a later analysis.

A data.table subset with a logical, for example CFG$table[group == "a"], adds an index to the table in place. Copy the table first with data.table::copy(), or set options(datatable.auto.index = FALSE) in the project. pbn sets neither.

The check has these limits:

  • It does not see a function inside an object, because R compiles a function after some calls.

  • It does not see the contents of an environment inside an object, for example that of a formula. It does not call an active binding.

  • It does not see a change of an object that already was in the global environment, other than an object of the functions folder.

  • The analysis that made the change fails, and the change stays in that R session. The run stops at that failure, see run_plan().

  • Without initialize_project(), pbn checks no object.

The check costs time in proportion to the size of the objects. One computer took about 45 microseconds for each analysis with a CFG of 49 elements. These held 5 data.tables of 100 rows, 20 KB in serialize().

For each scenario and simulation, pbn also adds one analysis named <scenario>__sim_<kkkk>__pbn_n_rows. It counts the rows of each data element. save_results() stores the counts in manifest$n_rows_data, and leaves the analysis out of the results.

add_analyses() stops before it adds anything when an analysis of that name is in the plan already.

See also

vignette("pbn"), which builds and runs a small fake project.

Other plan: add_data(), cohort_data(), get_data(), progress(), run_plan()

Examples

CFG <- list(
  scenarios = data.frame(scenario = c("real", "null"), sims = c(1, 2)),
  outcomes = c("y1", "y2")
)
p <- plnr::Plan$new()
pbn::add_data(p, "d", fn = function(scenario, sim) {
  return(data.frame(y1 = stats::rnorm(5), y2 = stats::rnorm(5)))
})
pbn::add_analyses(
  p,
  pbn::scenarios(CFG),
  name = "means",
  fn = function(data, argset) {
    return(data.frame(mean = mean(data$d[[argset$outcome]])))
  },
  outcome = CFG$outcomes
)
pbn::get_argset(p, "null", 2, "means", 2)
#> $scenario
#> [1] "null"
#> 
#> $sim
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $analysis
#> [1] "means"
#> 
#> $seed
#> [1] 1380106697
#> 
#> $outcome
#> [1] "y2"
#>
